To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people's judgments of conditional probability depend on how they partition the sample space and how they count the resulting events, (2) people's judgments can be explained by assuming that they partition, edit, count, and report probabilities in the manner predicted by the partition-count model.
participants' judgments of conditional probability are influenced by irrelevant information, small variations in problem wordings, and grouping of events.
people evaluate conditional probabilities by editing out irrelevant information and counting the remaining events.

people are more likely to use the partition-edit-count heuristic than they are to use the more complex, but potentially more accurate, subjective sampling model.
